name: Mental Maths: 2-Digit × 1-Digit Multiplication
description: A KaTeX-enabled mental-arithmetic deck for multiplying a two-digit number by a one-digit number. It develops distributive multiplication, carrying through full partial products, multiplier-specific methods, nearby-base shortcuts, estimation, error detection, and strategy selection.
estimatedTime: 130–160 minutes for the first pass; then 10–15 minute review bursts

cards.term: 2-Digit × 1-Digit: What is the reliable default method?
cards.definition:
Split the 2-digit number into tens and ones, then multiply each part.

$$
\begin{aligned}
47\times6 \\
&=(40+7)\times6 \\
&=40\times6+7\times6 \\
&=240+42 \\
&=282
\end{aligned}
$$
This is the distributive property. It works for every 2-digit by 1-digit product.

Starting with the tens gives you a meaningful running total.

$$
\begin{aligned}
58\times7 \\
&=50\times7+8\times7 \\
&=350+56 \\
&=406
\end{aligned}
$$
It is usually easier mentally than imitating written multiplication from right to left.

cards.term: 2-Digit × 1-Digit: What does carrying mean in multiplication?
cards.definition:
A product such as 8 × 7 = 56 contains 5 tens and 6 ones.

$$
\begin{aligned}
78\times7 \\
&=70\times7+8\times7 \\
&=490+56 \\
&=546
\end{aligned}
$$
In a written method, the 5 tens are carried. In mental maths, keep the full partial product 56.

cards.term: 2-Digit × 1-Digit: When should you use repeated doubling?
cards.definition:
Use repeated doubling for × 4, × 8, and × 16.

$$
\begin{aligned}
36\times8 \\
36\times2&=72 \\
72\times2&=144 \\
144\times2&=288
\end{aligned}
$$
This can be faster than separate partial products.

Multiply by 10, then halve.

$$
\begin{aligned}
74\times5 \\
&=740\div2 \\
&=370
\end{aligned}
$$
For odd numbers, halve the tens result: 73 × 5 = 730 ÷ 2 = 365.

Use 9 = 10 − 1.

$$
\begin{aligned}
64\times9 \\
&=64\times10-64 \\
&=640-64 \\
&=576
\end{aligned}
$$
Use this when multiplying by 10 and subtracting once is easy.

Use 6 = 3 × 2, or use standard splitting.

$$
\begin{aligned}
48\times6 \\
&=48\times3\times2 \\
&=144\times2 \\
&=288
\end{aligned}
$$
Choose the method you can execute more reliably.

There is no universally superior shortcut. Use table recall and splitting.

$$
\begin{aligned}
43\times7 \\
&=40\times7+3\times7 \\
&=280+21 \\
&=301
\end{aligned}
$$
A strong 7-times table is more valuable than a gimmick.

Double three times.

$$
\begin{aligned}
27\times8 \\
27\times2&=54 \\
54\times2&=108 \\
108\times2&=216
\end{aligned}
$$
This is particularly fast when the number is even or produces easy doubles.

Triple by doubling and adding once.

$$
\begin{aligned}
46\times3 \\
&=46\times2+46 \\
&=92+46 \\
&=138
\end{aligned}
$$
For many learners, this is faster than recalling a large 3-table fact.

Estimate to catch an answer that is wildly wrong.

$$
\begin{aligned}
68\times7\approx70\times7=490
\end{aligned}
$$
So an exact answer near 476 is credible; 376 would need rechecking.

Repeated doubling.

$$
\begin{aligned}
48\times2&=96 \\
96\times2&=192
\end{aligned}
$$
This is lower effort than decomposing 48 into tens and ones.

Use 9 = 10 − 1.

$$
\begin{aligned}
67\times9 \\
&=670-67 \\
&=603
\end{aligned}
$$

cards.term: True or false: n × 8 can always be found by doubling n three times.

cards.term: True or false: n × 9 is always found by adding n to n × 10.
cards.definition:
False.

Because 9 = 10 − 1, subtract once:
n × 9 = n × 10 − n.
